Consult Summary:
- 26-year-old male with history of asthma presents with 3 hours of chest tightness, mild shortness of breath, wheeze, and non-productive cough following a recent cold.
- Ran out of inhalers 1 week ago; plan for rescue and preventer inhalers, short oral steroid course, spacer, rest, and safety-net advice.

Problem List:

Issue 1:
- Acute asthma exacerbation (likely viral-triggered)
  - Onset: Chest tightness began ~3 hours prior to consult.
  - Symptoms: Chest tightness (not pain), mild shortness of breath, wheeze, non-productive cough; cough slightly worse at night; exertional dyspnea on stairs; not short of breath at rest.
  - Recent illness: Cold last week with sore throat and runny nose; URI symptoms improving but cough persists.
  - Medication adherence: Ran out of Ventolin (salbutamol) and Clenil Modulite ~1 week ago; not used for the past week.
  - Past severity: Severe exacerbation in high school requiring hospital admission and intubation; none recently.
  - Exam/metrics: No vitals; no peak flow available (telehealth).
  - Family history: Father with asthma.
  - Management (per consult):
    - Prescriptions for Ventolin and Clenil Modulite to resume therapy.
    - Short course of oral steroids: patient advised to take two tablets each morning for 5 days (specific drug/strength not documented).
    - Spacer device to improve inhaler delivery; instructions provided.
    - Use Ventolin as needed; seek medical attention if needing Ventolin more often than every 3 hours.
    - Safety-net: seek care for worsening shortness of breath, chest tightness/pain, light-headedness.

Issue 2:
- Recent viral upper respiratory infection with lingering cough
  - Timeline: Cold last week; sore throat and runny nose now improved; cough persists.
  - No sputum production.
  - Likely trigger for asthma flare.

Issue 3:
- Atopy and environmental allergies
  - Current: Hay fever; dust allergy.
  - Past: Childhood eczema; childhood milk protein allergy.
  - Family history: Mother with eczema.

Medications:
- Ventolin (salbutamol) inhaler — dose/route/frequency not documented; planned PRN use discussed.
- Clenil Modulite (beclomethasone) inhaler — dose/route/frequency not documented; advised to resume (use in the morning mentioned).
- Oral steroid course: two tablets each morning for 5 days; specific drug/strength not documented.
- Spacer device prescribed (device, not a medication).

Allergies:
- No known drug allergies.
- Environmental: dust allergy; hay fever.

Past Medical History:
- Asthma.
- Childhood eczema.
- Childhood milk protein allergy.
- Prior severe asthma exacerbation in adolescence requiring hospital admission and intubation.

Social History:
- Was away at university last week; ran out of inhalers.
- Work: doctor advised rest and time off work; details of occupation not documented.
- Smoking status: not documented.
- Alcohol use: not documented.
- Living arrangements: not documented.

Preventative History:
- Not discussed: cervical screening, mammogram, prostate blood test, fecal occult blood test, bone mineral density, vaccinations, recent optometry review, skin check.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: not recorded.
- Telehealth assessment: patient reports no shortness of breath at rest; increased shortness of breath with stairs; chest tightness without chest pain; non-productive cough; subjective wheeze.
- No peak flow measurement available.

Plan:
- Provide prescriptions for Ventolin (salbutamol) inhaler and Clenil Modulite inhaler; supply spacer device.
- Start oral steroid course: two tablets each morning for 5 days (specific drug/strength not documented); patient counseled on potential side effects (mood changes, hyperglycemia, rash, nausea, headache).
- Resume preventer inhaler as advised; use Ventolin as needed.
- Rest; time off work suggested (patient may self-certify for the first 7 days).
- Safety-net: seek medical attention if requiring Ventolin more often than every 3 hours or if symptoms worsen (increasing shortness of breath, chest tightness/pain, light-headedness).
- No routine follow-up explicitly arranged in transcript.

Quality checks:
- Missing expected elements: vital signs; objective respiratory exam; peak flow/FEV1; inhaler doses/strengths and exact frequencies; name/strength of oral steroid; smoking and alcohol history; vaccination status; clear follow-up plan.
- Internal conflicts: none noted.
- Transcript quality: Minor audio issues with brief cut-outs; core clinical details and plan captured.
